name: Indianapolis
title: Investor Renovation Contractor in Indianapolis, IN | Genstone
metaDescription: Renovation contractor for Indianapolis investors: flips, BRRRR, rental turns, doubles, 203(k) and REO work across Marion County's bungalows and ranches.
intro:
Indianapolis rewards investors who know which side of a street they are buying on. The same Marion County zip code can hold a restored foursquare that sold to an owner-occupant and, two blocks over, a vacant double with a collapsed rear porch and no working furnace. Genstone Construction scopes and manages renovations for people who buy both kinds of houses: flippers working the Near Eastside and Fountain Square, BRRRR investors holding brick ranches in Warren and Wayne Townships, funds rolling up single-family rentals, and servicers clearing bank-owned inventory.

We start with a free Pre-Offer Rehab Review so you see a realistic repair budget and an ARV check before you commit capital. From there, a designated field manager runs the job with vetted, licensed Indianapolis-area contractors from our national network, handles permits through the city's Department of Business and Neighborhood Services, and ties every draw to work that is finished and documented. You do not pay up front, and you can follow progress without driving to the site.
housingStock:
Most of the investor inventory inside the old city limits was built between the 1890s and the late 1920s. Expect frame cottages and shotgun-style singles on narrow lots in Haughville, the Near Westside and Martindale-Brightwood; two-story foursquares and Craftsman bungalows along the streets around Garfield Park, Bates-Hendricks and Mapleton-Fall Creek; and larger Queen Anne and Italianate houses in Herron-Morton Place and the Old Northside. Indianapolis also has a deep supply of side-by-side doubles, two mirror-image units under one roof, which show up all over the Near Eastside, Fountain Square and the south side.

Those prewar houses usually sit on fieldstone or brick foundations with partial basements or crawlspaces, and that matters for your budget. Mortar washes out, sills rot where grade has crept up against the siding, and basements built for coal storage were never meant to stay dry. Original wiring is often knob-and-tube spliced into later circuits, supply lines are commonly galvanized, and the main drain is frequently cast iron or clay tile out to the alley or street.

Past the old city line, the Unigov townships filled in after the Second World War. Warren, Wayne, Lawrence, Perry and Decatur Townships are full of brick and frame ranches from the 1950s through the 1970s, many on slabs or crawlspaces, with tri-levels and split-levels mixed in. These are simpler rehabs structurally, but they carry their own era markers: asbestos in floor tile and duct wrap, aluminum branch wiring in some late-1960s and early-1970s builds, and original electrical panels that insurers and appraisers flag.

The practical takeaway is that an Indianapolis rehab budget depends more on the decade of construction than on the square footage. A small 1910 cottage can cost more to make sound than a larger 1962 ranch, because the older house needs foundation, electrical and drain work before any finish work makes sense.

commonIssues.title: Knob-and-tube and overloaded old circuits
commonIssues.body: Prewar houses in neighborhoods like Haughville, Garfield Park and the Near Eastside often still have live knob-and-tube wiring buried in plaster walls, tied into a later fuse box or an undersized panel. Insurers in Indiana commonly refuse to write a policy on it, and lenders follow the insurer. We price a full rewire or a documented partial rewire up front rather than discovering it when the drywall comes down, because the answer changes your demo plan and your schedule.

commonIssues.title: Wet fieldstone and brick basements
commonIssues.body: Indianapolis sits on glacial clay and till that holds water against foundation walls after heavy spring rain. Older fieldstone and brick basements weep, mortar joints wash out and efflorescence builds up along the walls. The fix is usually a combination of regrading, extended downspouts, repointing and, where the basement is meant to be used, interior drainage tile and a sump. Skipping the exterior water management and only painting the walls is the most common shortcut we see on prior flips.

commonIssues.title: Cast-iron and clay sewer laterals
commonIssues.body: Long lateral runs from older houses to the main often include clay tile joints that roots find quickly, especially under mature street trees on the north side. Cast-iron stacks inside the house scale and crack along the bottom. We recommend a camera inspection on any prewar purchase, because a collapsed lateral can turn into a street cut, and Citizens Energy Group and the city have rules about who owns which section of pipe and how the work is permitted.

commonIssues.title: Lead paint on pre-1978 trim and porches
commonIssues.body: Nearly every double and bungalow in the older neighborhoods carries layers of lead-based paint on windows, trim and porch elements. Federal RRP rules apply to renovation work on these houses, and rental investors using Section 8 or other assisted programs face lead-safe requirements before a unit can be leased. We plan window replacement, porch work and exterior paint with lead-safe practices, and we document it so you have records if the unit is inspected.

commonIssues.title: Vacancy damage and stripped mechanicals
commonIssues.body: Indianapolis has a large inventory of houses that sat empty through foreclosure or estate delays, particularly east and northwest of downtown. Copper supply lines, furnace components and condensers are frequently missing, and winter freeze damage splits whatever plumbing remains. A vacant-house scope here typically assumes new supply plumbing, a new furnace and condenser, and a full electrical check before anything cosmetic. We confirm what is actually present during the walkthrough rather than relying on listing photos.

investorMarket:
Fix-and-flip activity is strongest where owner-occupant buyers are already moving in: Fountain Square, Bates-Hendricks, Garfield Park, Irvington, Little Flower and the streets around Mapleton-Fall Creek. Comps there support buyer-grade kitchens and baths, refinished original floors and careful exterior work, and the margin comes from keeping the original character while replacing every system behind the walls.

Buy-and-hold investors tend to concentrate in Warren, Wayne and Lawrence Townships and the near-south side, where brick ranches and modest bungalows rent steadily and appraise in a range that makes refinancing practical. Those houses suit BRRRR and single-family rental strategies because their structure is simple and their finishes can be standardized across a portfolio.

Doubles are their own niche. On the Near Eastside and south side they are popular with investors who want two rents on one lot, and in gentrifying pockets some are converted back to single-family use for resale. The decision between those paths depends on comps, zoning and the condition of the shared systems.

The northwest and far east sides carry more vacant, bank-owned and tax-sale inventory. Prices there leave room for heavier rehabs, but resale buyers are more limited, so most investors hold rather than flip. Wherever you buy, the free Pre-Offer Rehab Review is designed to tell you which of those strategies the specific house and block will actually support.
permits:
Building, electrical, plumbing and HVAC permits in Indianapolis and the rest of consolidated Marion County are issued by the Department of Business and Neighborhood Services, commonly called BNS. Excluded cities such as Beech Grove, Lawrence, Speedway and Southport handle their own permitting, so confirm which jurisdiction a parcel sits in before scheduling work. Structural repairs, new or relocated plumbing, electrical service changes, new circuits, furnace and water heater replacements, roofing in many cases, and decks or porches with new framing typically need permits and inspections. Indianapolis also requires contractors pulling permits to hold the appropriate city contractor license, and plumbing work in Indiana must be performed under a state-licensed plumber.

Historic districts add a step. Exterior changes in districts overseen by the Indianapolis Historic Preservation Commission, including Irvington, Herron-Morton Place, the Old Northside, Lockerbie Square and Fletcher Place, need a Certificate of Appropriateness before work starts, which affects window, siding, porch and roofing choices. Our field managers pull permits, schedule rough and final inspections, and collect lien waivers from every trade so the file is complete when you sell or refinance.
climate: Central Indiana gets real winters, humid summers and a stormy spring, and each season shapes a rehab. Freeze-thaw cycles are hard on old masonry, so tuckpointing, foundation parging and concrete flatwork are best scheduled from spring through fall. Vacant houses bought in winter should be assumed to have frozen pipes until a pressure test says otherwise. Spring brings heavy rain and severe thunderstorms, which is when wet basements and roof leaks show themselves, and it is also hail and wind season, so roofs and gutters deserve close inspection on any purchase. Summer humidity makes attic ventilation and air conditioning matter for both resale and rentals, and it slows paint and drywall drying in houses without working HVAC. We sequence exterior work early in the warm months and keep interior trades moving through winter once the house is heated.

faqs.q: Do you work in the excluded cities like Beech Grove and Lawrence?
faqs.a: Yes. We coordinate renovations across Marion County and the surrounding counties, including Beech Grove, Lawrence, Speedway and Southport, as well as Hamilton, Hendricks and Johnson County suburbs. The main difference is paperwork: those cities run their own building departments, so permits, inspections and contractor registration go through them instead of BNS. Your field manager confirms the right jurisdiction for the parcel during the scope stage so the permit plan is correct from the first day.

faqs.q: Should I keep an Indianapolis double as two units or convert it?
faqs.a: It depends on the block. Where owner-occupant buyers are paying for restored single-family homes, a conversion can produce a stronger resale. Where rents are steady and resale buyers are thin, keeping two units usually gives better long-term returns. Zoning, the condition of shared systems, and what comparable doubles have sold for all matter. The Pre-Offer Rehab Review prices both plans so you can compare them before you buy.

faqs.q: How do you handle houses in Irvington or other historic districts?
faqs.a: We check the parcel against Indianapolis Historic Preservation Commission district maps before the scope is final. If it falls in a district, exterior items like windows, siding, porch rails and roofing are planned to meet the commission's guidelines and we allow time for the Certificate of Appropriateness. Interior work is generally unaffected. Planning for this up front avoids having to undo work that a staff reviewer or neighbor flags later.

faqs.q: Can you start a rehab while I am still out of state?
faqs.a: Yes, a large share of our clients never visit the property. Your field manager walks the house, sends photos and the written scope, and posts progress and milestone documentation as the work moves forward. Draws are released for completed work, and final billing comes after you review and approve the finished job. You stay informed without needing a local contact or a trip to Indianapolis.

fix-flip.title: Fix and Flip Contractor in Indianapolis, IN | Genstone
fix-flip.metaDescription: Fix and flip renovations in Indianapolis: bungalows and foursquares in Fountain Square, Garfield Park and Irvington, scoped to comps and finished to list fast.
fix-flip.h1: Fix and Flip Renovations in Indianapolis
fix-flip.intro: A profitable Indianapolis flip is usually a 1910s or 1920s house that looks tired on top and needs honest work underneath. Buyers touring Fountain Square, Garfield Park or Irvington expect original trim and hardwood alongside a new kitchen, and their inspectors are going to open the electrical panel and run a camera down the sewer. Genstone builds the scope around both audiences. We use the free Pre-Offer Rehab Review to price the systems work first, then size the finish package to the comps on that specific street, so you are not putting quartz and custom tile into a house whose buyers are shopping on price. A designated field manager keeps trades sequenced and permits moving through BNS, which keeps carrying costs from piling up while the house sits.

sections.h2: Matching finishes to Indianapolis comps, block by block
sections.body:
The spread between neighborhoods in Indianapolis is wide, and it can change inside a few blocks. A bungalow on a street near Garfield Park that has already turned over to owner-occupants will compete against renovated houses with refinished oak floors, painted original trim, a reworked kitchen and an updated bath with period-appropriate tile. A similar house a mile east may compete against investor-grade flips where buyers care more about new mechanicals and a clean inspection report than about restored details.

We pull the scope toward whatever the recent sales on that street reward. In Irvington or Little Flower, that often means saving and refinishing original features, rebuilding front porches properly and choosing light fixtures and hardware that suit the era. In parts of the south and east side, it means durable, attractive mid-range finishes and putting more of the budget into roof, HVAC and electrical so the house clears inspection without renegotiation. Two plans at different finish levels, each tied to an ARV, are a normal part of our estimate when the comps are mixed.

sections.h2: The systems work that kills Indianapolis flips at inspection
sections.body:
The deals that fall apart here usually fall apart over things the seller's agent cannot photograph. A buyer's inspector finds active knob-and-tube in an attic, a galvanized supply line with low pressure upstairs, or a clay lateral with root intrusion halfway to the street, and suddenly your buyer wants a large credit or walks.

On prewar flips we budget for a modern electrical service and panel and the removal or documented abandonment of old wiring, new PEX or copper supply lines, a camera inspection of the sewer lateral with repair or lining where needed, and a furnace and water heater that will pass a home inspection. On basements we fix water at the outside first with grading and downspouts, then deal with walls and floor. These items are not exciting, but they are what lets a buyer's inspection come back clean on a house built before the First World War, and that clean report is what protects your sale price.

sections.h2: Keeping Indianapolis carrying costs under control
sections.body:
Every week a flip spends under construction or waiting for an inspection adds interest, taxes, insurance and utilities to your basis. We control that with sequencing rather than shortcuts. Permits through the Department of Business and Neighborhood Services are pulled at the start, rough inspections are booked as soon as walls are open, and long-lead items like windows, cabinets and HVAC equipment are ordered from the approved scope rather than after demo.

If the house is in an Indianapolis Historic Preservation Commission district, we put the Certificate of Appropriateness application in at the beginning so exterior work is not stuck waiting. Your field manager posts progress so you can line up your listing agent, photographer and staging around a real completion date. Draws are released only for completed work, which keeps your lender comfortable and your capital working on the next deal instead of sitting in a contractor's account. On a spring listing, that planning is often what gets the house on the market before the summer buyers in Indianapolis start to thin out.

faqs.q: Which Indianapolis neighborhoods work best for flips?
faqs.a: Areas where owner-occupants are actively buying tend to support flip pricing: Fountain Square, Bates-Hendricks, Garfield Park, Irvington, Little Flower and parts of Mapleton-Fall Creek and Butler-Tarkington. That shifts block by block, so we look at the specific street's recent sales during the Pre-Offer Rehab Review rather than relying on neighborhood names alone. A strong neighborhood can still contain a weak block, and the reverse is true too.

faqs.q: Do you keep original woodwork and floors on older flips?
faqs.a: Where buyers on that street pay for it, yes. Refinishing original oak or pine floors and stripping or painting original trim can add more value than replacing it, especially in Irvington and around Garfield Park. Where trim is too damaged or lead-laden to save economically, we price replacement with profiles that suit the house so the result still reads as period-appropriate.

faqs.q: Can you give me two flip budgets for the same house?
faqs.a: Yes. When the comps support it, we often provide two scopes: a moderate finish level priced against the middle of the comps and a higher one priced against the best recent sales. Each comes with its own ARV assumption, labor and material breakdown and draw schedule, so you can decide which plan fits your purchase price and timeline. Both plans share the same systems work, so only the finish budget changes between them.

brrrr.title: BRRRR Rehab Contractor in Indianapolis, IN | Genstone
brrrr.metaDescription: BRRRR rehabs in Indianapolis built to appraise and rent: brick ranches in Warren and Wayne Townships, south-side bungalows and doubles, finished for refinance.
brrrr.intro: Indianapolis is one of the Midwest markets where the BRRRR math can still work, but only if the rehab is built for two inspections at once: the appraiser's and the next ten years of tenants. Most of our Indianapolis BRRRR clients buy brick ranches in Warren, Wayne and Lawrence Townships, modest bungalows on the south side, or doubles on the Near Eastside. Genstone scopes those projects so the finished house supports the refinance appraisal while using materials that hold up to turnover. Our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review checks whether the repair budget and the likely appraisal leave enough room to pull your capital back out. Genstone Financial, a sister company, also offers DSCR rental loans if you want the refinance and the renovation coordinated under one roof.

sections.h2: Renovating to the Indianapolis refinance appraisal
sections.body:
An appraiser valuing a rental in Marion County compares it against recent sales of similar houses, not against what you spent. That means the scope should bring the house in line with the better-maintained comps in its township or neighborhood, then stop. In a 1950s brick ranch in Warren Township, that usually looks like a new roof where needed, updated electrical panel, functioning HVAC, a clean modern kitchen with durable counters, a refreshed bath, consistent flooring and fresh paint throughout.

Items that appraisers in this market consistently notice include full kitchens and baths in good condition, an absence of deferred maintenance on the exterior, a working furnace and air conditioner, and a finished, safe basement where one exists. Items that rarely move the appraisal include high-end tile, designer fixtures and elaborate landscaping. We document every upgrade with photos and an itemized completion list so you can hand the appraiser a clear record of what was replaced and when, which helps on a house whose listing photos still show the before condition.

A BRRRR house is a rental for years after the refinance closes, so the second half of the scope is about durability. We favor luxury vinyl plank in kitchens, baths and main living areas because it handles water and pets better than laminate or carpet. Paint colors and sheens are standardized so touch-ups between tenants are simple. Fixtures are commonly available models a maintenance tech can replace without special ordering.

Indianapolis-specific durability items matter too. Basements in older south-side bungalows need water management outside before any finish goes in below grade. Brick ranches in the townships often have original cast-iron drain lines under the slab or in the crawlspace, and it is cheaper to camera and repair them during the rehab than to chase backups with a tenant in place. Gutters, downspout extensions and grading protect foundations through wet springs. Keeping a house dry and simple is the difference between a rental that runs itself and one that eats its cash flow in service calls.

Side-by-side doubles are a natural fit for investors who want more rent per closing. On the Near Eastside, the south side and parts of the west side, a double with two separate entrances, two kitchens and two baths can produce stronger income than a single-family house at a similar purchase price.

The complication is that doubles often have tangled systems. We regularly see a single water service feeding both units, one electrical service split by a subpanel, and one furnace serving both sides through shared ductwork. For a rental you want each side separately metered for electric and gas where practical, each with its own heat source, so tenants pay their own utilities and one tenant's thermostat does not set the other's. Separating systems adds to the scope, and the Pre-Offer Rehab Review prices it so you can see whether the improved rents justify the cost before you buy. Appraisers valuing a double for the refinance also look at its income, which rewards that separation.

faqs.q: Does Genstone coordinate the refinance as well as the rehab?
faqs.a: Genstone Construction handles the renovation. Genstone Financial, a sister company within the Genstone Companies, offers DSCR rental loans along with fix-and-flip loans and lines of credit. You are free to use any lender, but if you want the rehab documentation and the refinance coordinated together, we can connect you with Genstone Financial early in the project, ideally before you close on the Indianapolis purchase.

faqs.q: What kind of Indianapolis houses make the best BRRRR projects?
faqs.a: Simple, solid structures in stable rental areas. Brick ranches from the 1950s and 1960s in Warren, Wayne and Lawrence Townships are common choices because they have fewer structural surprises than prewar houses. South-side bungalows and Near Eastside doubles can work very well, though older foundations and shared systems add scope that has to be priced in. The Pre-Offer Rehab Review shows that scope before you commit.

faqs.q: How do you document a BRRRR rehab for the appraiser?
faqs.a: We keep dated before, during and after photos, an itemized list of replaced systems and finishes, and copies of permits and final inspections from BNS. That package gives your appraiser and lender a clear picture of the renovation, which matters when public listing photos still show the house in its pre-rehab condition. You can forward the package directly or we can send it to your loan officer.

rental-renovation.title: Rental Property Renovation in Indianapolis | Genstone
rental-renovation.metaDescription: Single-family rental renovations in Indianapolis for funds and portfolio owners: standard scopes, durable finishes and tenant-ready turns in Marion County.
rental-renovation.intro: Indianapolis has drawn institutional single-family rental owners for years, and their houses sit side by side with those of local investors who own a handful of doors. The renovation needs are similar for both: houses that pass a move-in inspection, survive a tenant turnover without a gut, and do not generate emergency calls in January. Genstone Construction renovates rental homes across Marion County and the surrounding suburbs, from first-time stabilizations of newly acquired properties to routine turns between residents. Our field managers work from portfolio standards you set, our estimators price each property line by line, and Genstone Field Services can take over turn and make-ready work and occupied maintenance once the house is leased.

sections.h2: Portfolio standards across Marion County housing types
sections.body:
A rental portfolio in Indianapolis rarely contains one kind of house. A typical owner might hold a 1920s frame bungalow near Garfield Park, a 1960s brick ranch in Warren Township and a 1990s vinyl-sided two-story in Pike or Decatur Township. A single specification has to flex across all three.

We help owners set a standard that is consistent where it can be and adapted where it has to be. Flooring, paint, cabinet lines, counter material, plumbing fixtures, lighting and appliance packages can be identical across the portfolio, which simplifies purchasing and future maintenance. Systems decisions vary by era: the older bungalow likely needs electrical and supply plumbing replaced, the ranch may need its original panel and cast-iron drains addressed, and the newer house may only need a mechanical tune-up. Writing those distinctions into the scope keeps your per-door budget honest and keeps a property manager from inheriting problems the renovation should have fixed.

Indianapolis rentals take wear from winters, wet springs and turnover, and the scope should reflect all three. Furnaces and water heaters get replaced when they are near the end of their life rather than when they fail on a cold night with a tenant in place. Exterior doors and windows are sealed tightly because drafty prewar houses drive high utility bills that push tenants out at lease end. In basements, we address grading and downspouts before touching interior finishes, because a single wet spring can ruin carpet or drywall below grade.

Inside, we lean on hard-surface flooring, semi-gloss on trim and doors, solid-surface or laminate counters with sealed edges, and fixtures that a maintenance tech can source locally. For houses built before 1978, lead-safe work practices apply during renovation, and any owner leasing to voucher holders should expect lead-related inspection requirements. Planning for those up front avoids failing a move-in inspection after the work is done.

Once a rental is stabilized, the next scope is the turn. A tenant moves out, and the owner needs the house cleaned, repaired, repainted where needed and back on the market quickly. Genstone Field Services, part of the Genstone Companies, handles turn and make-ready work, inspections and occupied maintenance, so the same organization that renovated the house can keep it tenant-ready.

For Indianapolis portfolios that means a consistent move-out inspection, a written scope priced against your standard, photos of damage for deposit disputes, and a make-ready completed by vetted local contractors. Because the original renovation used standard materials, matching paint, flooring and fixtures during a turn is straightforward. Our one-year workmanship warranty covers the work we performed, while tenant damage and normal wear are handled as turn scope. Owners get documentation at every step, which helps with both internal reporting and conversations with residents about deposits. That paper trail becomes more valuable as an Indianapolis portfolio grows past what one owner can personally inspect.

faqs.q: Can you renovate rentals that are currently occupied?
faqs.a: Yes. Occupied work in Indianapolis is scheduled with notice to residents, kept to defined areas, and sequenced so the household keeps a working kitchen, bath and heat whenever possible. Genstone Field Services also handles occupied maintenance for portfolio owners, so smaller repairs can be handled between renovations without a separate vendor. In winter we avoid shutting off heat in an occupied Indianapolis house for longer than a single working day.

faqs.q: Do you work with property managers as well as owners?
faqs.a: Yes. Many Indianapolis portfolio owners have a local property manager who handles leasing and residents. We can take scopes and approvals from either the owner or the manager, send progress documentation to both, and coordinate access through the manager so tenants hear from one familiar contact. Scope changes still go to whoever you designate as the approver, and nothing outside the approved scope is billed without that sign-off.

faqs.q: How do you price a rental renovation across many houses?
faqs.a: Each property gets its own itemized estimate, but the line items and finishes come from a shared standard, so pricing is consistent and easy to compare. Systems work is priced house by house based on age and condition. Dumpster and debris costs are included, and draws follow completed work. Owners can compare a Warren Township ranch and a south-side bungalow line by line and see exactly why one costs more.

multifamily-renovation.title: Duplex & Double Renovation Contractor Indianapolis | Genstone
multifamily-renovation.metaDescription: Renovation of Indianapolis doubles, duplexes and small 2-4 unit buildings: shared-system separation, phased occupied work and permits through BNS.
multifamily-renovation.intro: When investors here talk about small multifamily, they usually mean the Indianapolis double: a side-by-side house with two mirror-image units, common across the Near Eastside, Fountain Square, the south side and the near west side. The city also has a scattering of up-and-down duplexes, small brick fourplexes from the 1920s near the old streetcar lines, and converted Victorians carved into units in neighborhoods north of downtown. Genstone Construction renovates all of them for investors who want income from two to four units under one roof. We specialize in the parts that make these buildings harder than single-family work: separating shared utilities, phasing work around occupied units, and handling fire separation, egress and permits correctly so the building is safe and financeable.

sections.h2: Untangling shared systems in Indianapolis doubles
sections.body:
Many Indianapolis doubles were built with separate units but shared infrastructure, and decades of owner repairs often made the tangle worse. A typical walkthrough finds one water meter, one sewer lateral, a single gas meter and an electrical service that was split with a subpanel or a few added circuits rather than true separate metering. Heating is sometimes a single old furnace with ducts running to both sides, or two furnaces in a shared basement drawing from one gas line.

For an income property, separate electric and gas meters and an independent heat source for each unit are worth pricing seriously because they shift utility costs to tenants and make each side easy to manage. Water usually stays on one meter. We coordinate with AES Indiana and Citizens Energy Group on new services, size panels for modern loads, and lay out new ductwork so each unit controls its own comfort. That separation is often the single largest line item in a double renovation, and the Pre-Offer Rehab Review is where we tell you how big it is likely to be.

sections.h2: Fire separation, egress and code in older Indianapolis buildings
sections.body:
Older doubles and converted houses rarely have the separation between units that modern code expects. Shared attics, open basements and party walls built with plaster on lath and gaps around pipes let smoke and fire move between units. When a renovation opens walls or changes layouts, inspectors from the Department of Business and Neighborhood Services will look for proper fire separation where work is being done.

We plan for that from the start. Typical items include fire-rated drywall on the common wall and at the ceiling between units, fire blocking at the attic, sealed penetrations, hardwired interconnected smoke alarms in each unit, carbon monoxide alarms near sleeping areas, and egress windows in bedrooms. Converted Victorians north of downtown can be trickier, with second-floor units that rely on a single rear stair. Getting these items right protects tenants, keeps the building insurable and avoids failed inspections that stall a project. It also helps when a lender or insurer asks how the units are separated.

Many investors buy a double or fourplex with one or more units leased, and the rents from occupied units help carry the building while the vacant one is renovated. We phase work to make that possible: the vacant unit is completed first, then a tenant can move over or the next unit is turned when its lease ends.

Work that affects the whole building, such as a new electrical service, roof replacement, sewer lateral repair or a gas line change, is scheduled with advance notice and kept as short as possible. Shared basements are cleaned up and secured so tenants are not living next to an open job site. In winter, heat stays on in occupied units throughout. Your field manager handles resident communication through your property manager if you have one, and posts progress and photos so you can see each phase finish before the next one starts. Occupied units keep producing rent the whole way through.

faqs.q: Is it worth separately metering an Indianapolis double?
faqs.a: Often, yes, but the answer depends on the building and the rents. Separate electric and gas meters let tenants pay their own utilities and make heating complaints simpler to resolve. The cost of new services, panels and furnaces can be significant, so we price separation against your rent assumptions during the Pre-Offer Rehab Review before you buy. On some Indianapolis doubles, separate electric is easy and separate heat is not, so we price each piece on its own.

faqs.q: Can a double be converted to a single-family house?
faqs.a: In many Indianapolis neighborhoods, yes, and it is a common move where owner-occupants are buying. Zoning, the building layout and the cost of combining two kitchens and two sets of stairs all matter. We can price both a two-unit rental scope and a single-family conversion so you can compare them. Removing a second kitchen and meter is usually straightforward; reworking two front entries into one takes more thought.

faqs.q: Do you handle fourplexes and converted houses too?
faqs.a: Yes. We work on two- to four-unit buildings of all kinds, including brick fourplexes and older houses divided into apartments. Those buildings usually need more attention to fire separation, egress and stairways, and we plan that scope with permits through the Department of Business and Neighborhood Services. Converted Victorians around Herron-Morton Place may also need historic commission review for exterior stair or window changes.

fha-203k.title: FHA 203(k) Contractor in Indianapolis, IN | Genstone
fha-203k.metaDescription: FHA 203(k) certified contractor in Indianapolis: Standard and Limited rehab bids, consultant coordination and lender draws on bungalows, doubles and ranches.
fha-203k.intro: The FHA 203(k) loan lets an Indianapolis buyer finance both the purchase and the renovation of a house in one mortgage, and it fits this city better than most. Marion County is full of sound but dated 1920s bungalows, 1950s brick ranches and owner-occupied doubles that will not pass a standard FHA appraisal as-is but make excellent homes after repairs. Genstone Construction is an FHA 203(k) Certified Contractor. We prepare the detailed bids, line-item scopes and draw schedules that lenders and 203(k) consultants need, and we manage the work through completion. Buyers, buyer's agents and loan officers in Indianapolis use us to keep 203(k) transactions on schedule, because a contractor who understands the paperwork is what keeps these closings from stalling.

sections.h2: Standard or Limited 203(k) for an Indianapolis house
sections.body:
The two versions of the program fit different houses. The Limited 203(k) covers minor remodeling and nonstructural repairs with total rehabilitation costs up to $75,000. For projects over $15,000 an inspection is required, and a 203(k) consultant is optional unless the lender requires one. In Indianapolis, the Limited program suits a 1960s ranch in Lawrence or Warren Township that needs a new furnace, roof, kitchen and flooring, or a south-side bungalow that needs paint, windows and a bath.

The Standard 203(k) is for bigger or structural projects. Rehabilitation costs must total at least $5,000, and an FHA-approved 203(k) consultant is required. That is the right path for a prewar house in Garfield Park or the Near Eastside needing foundation repair, a full rewire, a new sewer lateral, or a reconfigured floor plan. We look at the house with the buyer and agent and recommend the version that fits the actual scope, rather than squeezing a structural job into the Limited program.

sections.h2: Which Indianapolis houses fit the 203(k) well
sections.body:
The best 203(k) candidates here are houses that are structurally sound but have problems a standard FHA appraisal will flag: missing or failing mechanicals, peeling lead-based paint, roof leaks, broken windows, unsafe stairs or handrails, or outdated electrical. That describes a lot of Marion County inventory, from estate-sale bungalows in Beech Grove and University Heights to dated ranches on the east side.

Indianapolis doubles are worth a specific mention. FHA allows owner-occupied two- to four-unit properties, so a buyer can live in one side of a double and rent the other, using 203(k) financing to renovate both. That can be an attractive first purchase. Houses we usually steer buyers away from are those with major foundation failure, significant fire damage or heavy unpermitted additions, where the costs and approvals can push the project beyond what the loan and the buyer's timeline can support. When a house is borderline, we say so during the walkthrough so the buyer and agent can keep looking before spending on appraisals.

sections.h2: Bids, consultants and draws on Indianapolis 203(k) loans
sections.body:
A 203(k) moves on documentation. The lender needs a contractor bid broken out line by line, often matched to the consultant's write-up, plus our license and insurance information. We prepare those bids in the format lenders expect, coordinate with the 203(k) consultant on the work write-up, and update the scope if the appraisal or consultant changes it.

After closing, renovation funds are released in draws as work is completed and inspected. Our field manager schedules work so each draw corresponds to a clear milestone, collects lien waivers from trades, and handles permits and inspections through BNS or the relevant excluded city. Lead-safe work practices are used on pre-1978 houses, which covers most of the older Indianapolis stock. The buyer sees progress and documentation throughout, and final payment follows completion and the buyer's approval of the finished work. If an inspector or consultant finds hidden conditions once walls are open, we document them and work through the lender's change-order process rather than proceeding on a handshake. That protects the contingency reserve the loan sets aside for exactly this kind of surprise in older Indianapolis homes.

faqs.q: Can I use a 203(k) loan on an Indianapolis double?
faqs.a: Yes, if you plan to live in one unit. FHA allows owner-occupied properties with up to four units, and Indianapolis doubles are a common choice. The renovation can cover both sides, and the rent from the second unit can help with the monthly payment. Your lender will confirm eligibility and how rental income is counted. Separating utilities between the two sides can be included in the renovation budget.

faqs.q: Do you work directly with Indianapolis loan officers and agents?
faqs.a: Yes. We regularly send bids and documentation straight to the lender and consultant, and we keep the buyer's agent updated on scope and timing so the closing date stays realistic. Having the contractor and the paperwork aligned early is what keeps a 203(k) transaction from stalling in underwriting. We can usually schedule the walkthrough during the buyer's inspection period so the bid is ready when the lender asks for it.

faqs.q: What happens if the consultant adds items to my scope?
faqs.a: That is common, especially on older Indianapolis houses where the consultant flags safety or health items like electrical hazards, handrails or peeling paint. We revise the bid to include the added items, keep it consistent with the consultant's write-up, and resubmit to the lender so the loan reflects the true renovation cost. If the added items push a Limited loan past its limits, we explain the options with your loan officer.

reo-renovation.title: REO & Bank-Owned Renovation in Indianapolis | Genstone
reo-renovation.metaDescription: REO renovation for servicers, banks and GSEs in Indianapolis: freeze damage, mold, stripped mechanicals and code violations on vacant Marion County homes.
reo-renovation.h1: REO and Bank-Owned Property Renovations in Indianapolis
reo-renovation.intro: Indianapolis carries a steady flow of vacant and bank-owned homes, and many of them arrive in rough shape. A foreclosure that sat empty through an Indiana winter can come with burst pipes, missing copper, a gutted furnace and mold in the basement, plus open code enforcement cases from neighbors who reported tall grass or broken windows. Genstone Construction works with mortgage servicers, banks, REITs, investment funds and Government-Sponsored Enterprises to bring REO properties in Marion County back to marketable condition. Genstone is a preferred contractor for GSEs, and our sister company Genstone Field Services handles property preservation, inspections and code compliance, so a property can go from securing and winterizing to full renovation without changing vendors.

sections.h2: What vacant Indianapolis homes typically look like
sections.body:
The condition of an Indianapolis REO depends heavily on how long it sat and whether it was winterized properly. The most common findings are freeze damage to supply lines, water heaters and boilers; missing copper plumbing, condensers and furnace parts taken by thieves; roof leaks that soaked attic insulation and ceilings; and mold in basements and crawlspaces where moisture had nowhere to go.

Older houses on the east and northwest sides also frequently arrive with broken windows, damaged doors from forced entry, accumulated trash and debris, and overgrown yards. Brick ranches in the townships tend to hold up better structurally, but they still lose mechanicals and flooring when water gets in. We start every REO with a full walkthrough, photo documentation and a pressure test of the supply plumbing so the scope reflects actual damage rather than assumptions from a drive-by inspection. We also check whether utilities are active, because restoring service in Indianapolis sometimes requires repairs and a passed inspection before the utility will reconnect.

sections.h2: Code enforcement and the Indianapolis permit path for REO
sections.body:
Vacant homes in Indianapolis tend to accumulate code violations: high weeds, open structures, trash, unsafe exterior stairs, and in some cases unsafe building orders. Inspectors with the Department of Business and Neighborhood Services cite owners and can escalate to fines and repair orders. When a servicer or bank takes title, those cases come with the property.

Genstone Field Services handles code compliance work and coordinates with Genstone Construction so open violations are resolved as part of the renovation plan. Our field managers pull permits for electrical, plumbing, mechanical and structural repairs, schedule inspections and keep documentation tied to each violation so the case can be closed. For properties in historic districts like Irvington or the Old Northside, we account for Indianapolis Historic Preservation Commission review on any exterior work. A clean code file and finished permits make the home easier to sell and keep it from lingering on a violation list.

sections.h2: Renovation scopes built for REO disposition
sections.body:
Servicers and banks usually want one of a few outcomes: a property repaired to a level where it can be sold quickly to an owner-occupant, a property brought to FHA or conventional financing standards, or a limited repair package that resolves health, safety and code issues before sale to an investor. We write scopes to whichever strategy the client chooses, with clear line items so asset managers can compare options.

In Indianapolis, a retail-ready REO scope commonly includes restoring water and heat, roof repair or replacement, mold remediation, new flooring and paint, kitchen and bath updates and exterior cleanup. A financing-ready scope focuses on the items an FHA or conventional appraiser will call out. Every scope includes dumpster and debris costs, lien waivers and before-and-after documentation, which helps with internal approvals and investor reporting. Our designated field manager stays on the property from the first walkthrough until final billing. Asset managers get one contact for every Indianapolis property in their queue.

faqs.q: Do you handle preservation as well as renovation on Indianapolis REO?
faqs.a: Yes, through the Genstone Companies. Genstone Field Services provides property preservation, inspections, occupied maintenance, turn and make-ready, and code compliance. Genstone Construction handles the renovation scope. Using both keeps the property history, photos and documentation in one place from the initial secure through the finished rehab. For servicers managing many Indianapolis assets, that continuity reduces the number of handoffs where photos or notes get lost.

faqs.q: How do you deal with freeze damage in vacant Indianapolis homes?
faqs.a: We pressure-test the plumbing during the first walkthrough to find every leak, check water heaters and boilers, and inspect for ceiling and floor damage below failed lines. Most freeze-damaged houses need new supply plumbing and often a new water heater. We then address any resulting mold before closing up walls. If the house will sit again before sale, we winterize it properly once the new plumbing passes inspection.

faqs.q: Can you resolve open code violations on bank-owned homes?
faqs.a: Yes. We review the open cases with the asset manager, include the corrective work in the renovation scope, pull the required permits through the Department of Business and Neighborhood Services, and provide documentation to help close each case. That avoids escalating fines and helps the property sell. Exterior items like weeds and boarding can often be handled first, while interior permits are in review.
